extracted.intended_audience: general readers; student journalists, educators, and legal advocates interested in student press rights
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes legal standards, typical practices, and protections concerning suppression of student-run news operations in the United States, including key Supreme Court decisions, state 'New Voices' laws, common censored topics, and examples of administrative actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of censorship of student media
rubrics_metrics.description: The censorship of student media in the United States is the suppression of student-run news operations' free speech by school administrative bodies, typically state schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes schools using authority to control funding and distribution of publications, taking down articles, and preventing distribution. Also extends to confiscating independently produced underground publications or imposing discipline for material posted on off-campus websites. (Article opening paragraphs and examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier (1988) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court held that student newspapers do not have the same freedoms and safeguards as professional media and that public school curricular student newspapers that have not been established as forums for student expression are subject to a lower level of First Amendment protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because curricular papers were deemed not public forums, administrators may regulate content; censorship permitted when related to legitimate pedagogical concerns. Example: Hazelwood East High School withheld articles on abortion and divorce. The decision prompted states to pass counteracting legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishment of First Amendment rights of students in U.S. public schools; student expression is protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting student speech is only justified if it would materially and substantially disrupt school operations (the 'substantial disruption' test). Tinker is a foundational precedent applied in later student-speech cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papish v. Board of Curators of University of Missouri (1973) protection
rubrics_metrics.description: A Supreme Court ruling that the University of Missouri could not discipline a college student for profanity and 'indecent' sexual references in an 'underground' publication that she funded and distributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates greater protection for independent college student expression compared with regulated curricular publications; illustrates limits on university discipline for off-campus/independent student publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rosenberger v. University of Virginia (1995) — funding/viewpoint principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court assessment on whether a state university may withhold funding of student publications with regard to the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses viewpoint discrimination and the constitutional implications of denying funding to student-sponsored publications because of content. Relevant for evaluating how institutional funding choices affect free-expression rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morse v. Frederick (2007) limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court decision concluding that speech promoting illegal drug use during school-sanctioned events is unprotected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes that some categories of student speech (e.g., advocating illegal drug use at school events) fall outside First Amendment protection and can be disciplined by schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum status (public forum vs school-sponsored/nonpublic forum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a student publication is established as a forum for student expression (by policy or practice) determines its level of First Amendment protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public/forum status affects review standard: independent or formally recognized forums receive greater protection than curricular publications not opened as forums. Hazelwood contrasted curricular/non-forum papers with independent forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate pedagogical concern standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Hazelwood, schools may censor student speech for 'legitimate pedagogical concern.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'legitimate pedagogical concern' lacks a clear definition, it has been interpreted variably; this ambiguity led some states to pass laws that explicitly define when and where administration can censor student media and to offer protections for school employees who support student speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Voices legislation protections
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws (branded 'New Voices') enacted to fortify student journalists' right to free expression and to counteract Hazelwood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By 2013 and continuing through later years, multiple states passed New Voices laws clarifying limits on administrative censorship and protecting advisers; the article lists states that have adopted such legislation and notes the Student Press Law Center's advocacy role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical censored topics in student media
rubrics_metrics.description: Topics commonly censored based on interviews and survey data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes sexual assault, politics, athletics, women's reproductive rights, the #MeToo movement; other reported examples in cases include pornography, LGBTQ issues, and reporting on COVID-19 vaccine mandates or staff. The article cites survey/finding that many student newspapers face some form of censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of administrative censorship/actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific administrative actions that constitute censorship of student media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the article: removing/taking down articles, shutting down websites or entire newspapers, controlling funding/distribution, preventing publication of specific stories or editorials, suspending or threatening to fire faculty advisers, and confiscating independently produced 'underground' publications. Case examples and news reports illustrate these tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of censorship on student civic life
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship of student media obstructs student activism and undermines democratic engagement among students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains that removal or suppression of student outlets diminishes cohesion, attacks sharing of opinions and information, and 'delegitimizes democracy' by reducing belief that the school is responsive to student wishes. This dimension can be used to evaluate broader harms from censorship beyond legal compliance.
